text: Eleven years ago Fernando Tobajas moved into his bathroom and has not come out since. He has furnished it, more or less, into an apartment. Friends still visit, so the room stays social, and he keeps up a practice no saner arrangement would permit: messages rolled into aspirin tubes and sent down the toilet, on the chance that someone downstream will learn he exists. Juan Estelrich March shot this in Spain in 1977, and the 108 minutes press almost entirely into one tiled room, which throws the weight onto talk, onto the patience of the visitors, and onto a man who has surrendered everything except his opinion of himself. Then Arabel Lee finds one of the tubes. The arrangement he spent a decade perfecting acquires the one thing it was not built to survive: an answer.

A television reporter comes to a Swiss village to interview a man who studies world hunger, and stays for a road accident. The dead man is an Italian immigrant worker named Mario Ricci, and the account of how he died does not hold together. Claude Goretta keeps both jobs inside the same week: the scheduled programme, with its expert and its lights, and the unscheduled questions nobody in a small place wants from someone who will be gone by Friday. The reporter has a camera, an assistant, and no standing here. What he can get depends on who is willing to talk to an outsider, and on how much local goodwill he is prepared to spend, given that he still needs it for the programme he came to shoot. The interview and the inquiry compete for the same days, and only one of them has a broadcast date.

Maria holds a job, does the cooking and the cleaning, and studies on top of it. Her father is blind and drinks, and when he drinks he beats her mother. Her brothers reach the limit of what they can stand to watch and leave the house. Maria stays, because the household runs on her and everyone in it, Maria included, has quietly agreed to that. Teresa Villaverde made Três Irmãos in Portugal in 1994, and the film is patient about the least dramatic part of the situation: the meals still get made, the shifts still get worked, the studying still has to happen at some hour of the night. Violence in that house is not an event but a climate. What the film watches is what the carrying costs the one person who was never offered the exit her brothers took.

Hong Kong, 1976: a life of Bruce Lee assembled from the vantage of the woman who had no public claim on him. The first person in the title is hers. Eighty-seven minutes is short for a life and about right for a claim, and the picture is catalogued as action, which states the terms of the exchange plainly: the fighting sells the ticket, the intimacy justifies the billing. So what is on offer is less a biography than a position, a very public body described by a witness who was kept outside the public account of it. The fame is never argued for, only assumed, because everyone buying a ticket in 1976 already held it. That leaves the film one asset, which is also its problem: nearness to a man the audience already believed it knew.

The war ends, and the work of punishing collaborators begins. Jutro opens in those first days of peace in Yugoslavia and hands them to a former partisan, so its subject is not fighting but the administration of victory: names, lists, a weapon still issued, men sorting neighbours they stood beside a week ago. Seventy-six minutes, with no room in it for anything to be softened by length. Mladomir 'Puriša' Đorđević made the film in 1967, at a distance from those weeks long enough for the survivors to have households and short enough for them to remember exactly who did what to whom. What was courage last month is procedure this month, carried out by the same hands. For the man carrying it, peace is simply where the war went to continue under another name.

The old man cannot leave his bed, so he has angled mirrors until the whole house reports back to him. From there a former sailor keeps his grip on two possessions: the property, and his son, who is conducting an affair with the widow next door and would prefer it went unobserved. Silvio Caiozzi filmed this in Chile in 1990, seventy-five minutes, largely indoors, with surveillance built into the furniture. The mechanism is domestic and perfectly legal — an illness, a duty, some tilted glass — and it works only because the son consents to it every day. A chamber piece of that size went out as Chile's international submission to the Academy Awards. What holds attention is the calculation the son makes each evening, weighing the widow against a man who sees every room without turning his head.

A woman leaves her small son with an old boyfriend for three days. Eli agrees to it, and then spends those days on the exact line between minding the boy and wanting him hurt, with the film declining to settle which he is. Uri Zohar made it in Israel in 1967 from a story by Abraham B. Jehoshua, ninety minutes, and the material stays almost entirely interior: an ordinary stretch of days, a child who needs watching, and a man conducting an argument with an absent woman by way of a boy who has no idea he is in one. Three days is short enough that nothing has time to harden into a plan. Oded Kotler plays Eli, and the discomfort is not that anything is being arranged. It is that the impulse and the care arrive in the same minute, and neither one holds the room for long.

Setting up the carousel, a fairground worker digs into a skeleton, a steel helmet, and a machine gun. The village is German and the year in the film is 1959; the bones are Robert Mertens, an ordinary soldier who deserted in 1944 and walked home to ask for help. Wolfgang Staudte cuts between the fair going up and what happened at those doors — former friends, then the minister, then his own parents, each performing a small private calculation about what a deserter in the kitchen would cost them. That is where the whole thing takes place: in kitchens, at a normal volume, among people who are not villains by trade. Made in 1960, near enough to the arithmetic that everyone involved could still read it. Above the spot, meanwhile, the annual fair goes up on schedule.

A hotel room with one door, no windows, and nothing on the walls that gives back a reflection. A valet brings in Joseph Garcin, then Inès Serrano and Estelle Rigault, then locks up and goes. They work out where they are quickly enough; what they cannot work out is when the torture is due to start. While they wait they do the only available thing and talk: sins, appetites, the memories each would rather keep. Tad Danielewski filmed Jean-Paul Sartre's play in 1962 and gave it eighty-five minutes, which leaves a camera nowhere to go that the three of them cannot also go. The interest is mechanical rather than theological: people who cannot leave, cannot sleep, and cannot stop being looked at, discovering that this is already a complete apparatus and needs no staff.

In 1866 a Russian writer owed money he could not repay, and this film invents twenty-six days inside that year. The debts are the least of it. One journal had been shut down for political reasons and the next needed funding; a brother he was close to had died; a wife had died of tuberculosis; and Crime and Punishment, the book that would settle the question of who he was, had not yet arrived. Aleksandr Zarkhi gives the stretch eighty-seven minutes and files it under romance and history, a pairing that promises the private version of a public name and delivers something less flattering: the ordinariness of a very bad year from inside it, before any of it is legible as a life. A man owes money, has lost two people, and still has to produce pages by a date.

Larry Winters was convicted of murder, and the film made about him is catalogued as horror. That pairing is the difficulty in miniature. A crime picture usually runs on what was done and how it came to light, but here the doing is settled before the first frame and the man is already a matter of public record, which leaves eighty-five minutes to find something else to be about. David Hayman directed it in Britain in 1990, and the three labels attached to it — horror, crime, thriller — pull in three directions, which is roughly the range of positions available to anyone filming a killer who remains, inconveniently, a person. Where the camera stands is not a question of style here. It decides what the film is claiming about a man whose worst hour is already on the record.

Pietro's job is to catch shoplifters, and he is good enough at it to notice the day he lets one go. Her name is Pabe, she is Roma, and he cannot account for the decision. The rest of his week runs on a divorced man's timetable: the store, weekend visits to children who live with his ex-wife, and a flirtation with the makeup consultant that he rehearses more than he conducts. His body registers all of it in nosebleeds and sudden temper. Silvio Soldini takes 124 minutes over this and spends them slowly, on two people circling each other while neither settles what the other is for. They met inside an arrangement that had already assigned them parts — one paid to watch, one expected to be watched — and whatever follows has to be built out of the hours when neither is on duty.

The arrangement is an apartment: Janine lives in it, and the man paying for it is not her husband. Francois, who owns a factory and a marriage he does not want, set her up there and considers the matter settled. Janine finds the terms comfortable enough to keep when her own husband comes back from the war. So this is not a film about a secret. Everyone concerned knows the arithmetic and stays inside it anyway, and Claude Autant-Lara, in 1953, treats bourgeois adultery as a going concern with rent, hours and running costs. A hundred and five minutes of people who have priced one another. What keeps it from turning merely sour is the exactness of the accounting: nobody here is deceived for long, which means each of them has agreed, item by item, to what they are getting.

The boy hiding from the occupation and the man filming him are the same person. Michel Drach adapted his own childhood — a Jewish family in occupied France working out how to get away from it — and then put the grown filmmaker into the picture, unable to leave the material alone. The doubling is the structure rather than a flourish: the film keeps moving between the escape and the crew assembled decades later to reconstruct it, which sets a working film unit down in the middle of the worst thing that ever happened to the man employing it. France, 1974, a hundred and ten minutes. The wartime passages take the child's vantage, where adult terror arrives as an unexplained change of plan, and the later ones belong to a man who can hold the memory only by staging it and watching other people perform it.
